title: Why keyword search misses things
summary: People and documents use different words for the same thing, and keyword search only matches exact words. Patches like synonym lists and stemming help a little, but they never catch up. What you actually want is to match meaning.
html:
Lesson 3 ended with "How much holiday do I get?" scoring zero against a handbook that says "leave". Today is how often that happens, and why the usual fixes do not really fix it.

The core problem

The person asking and the person who wrote the document chose their words separately. They mean the same thing and say it differently. Keyword search only matches the exact same word, so every difference in wording is a miss. This has a name: vocabulary mismatch. Here are its three most common shapes.

Shape one: different words, same meaning

question says    document says
holiday          leave
work from home   remote work
laptop           company equipment
fired            terminated

Every row is a total miss for keyword search. And notice the last two rows: the person asking uses everyday words, while the document uses formal ones. That gap is the norm, not the exception, because handbooks and policies are written by people trying to sound official.

Shape two: same word, different form

Ask "Who approves leave?" Paragraph B says "approved". To a computer, "approves" and "approved" are just different strings of letters, so they do not match. B only scores for "leave".

The standard patch is to chop words down to a shared root before comparing: "approves", "approved" and "approving" all become "approv". That is called stemming. It helps with this shape and nothing else. It cannot turn "holiday" into "leave".

Shape three: same word, different meaning

This one goes the other way. Search for "leave" and you will also match "please leave the building by 6 pm". Same word, nothing to do with time off. Keyword search cannot tell, so it happily returns the wrong paragraph. Misses are bad; confident wrong matches are worse, because the AI then answers from the wrong text.

The obvious patch, and why it runs out

Keep a list: whenever someone writes "holiday", also look for "leave". It works, and the exercise below lets you see it work. But look at what it costs. Someone has to write that list. A company with thousands of documents has thousands of these pairs, they differ between teams, and new ones appear every month. Nobody keeps that list complete.

And even when it works, it only half works. With "holiday" mapped to "leave", paragraphs A and B both score 1. Both contain "leave", so keyword search has no way to tell that A is about how many days and B is about who signs off. A person would know instantly. The search does not.

The analogy: a very literal colleague who will only hand you a file if your request uses the exact words on its label. You can give them a cheat sheet of other names for things, but the sheet is never complete, and they still cannot tell which file actually answers your question.

What we actually want

We want the search to understand that "holiday" and "leave" mean nearly the same thing, without anyone writing that down. In other words, to match meaning instead of spelling. The way that is done is by turning meaning into numbers, which sounds strange and turns out to be simple. That is the next lesson.

New words today

Vocabulary mismatch: the question and the document use different words for the same thing, so keyword search misses.

Stemming: chopping words down to a shared root, so "approves" and "approved" match. It helps with word forms only.

Both are in the glossary.

If you remember one thing
Keyword search matches spelling, not meaning. People and documents say the same thing in different words all the time, and no list of synonyms ever keeps up.

Next lesson: turning words into numbers, so that similar meanings end up close together.
exercise:
Patch it yourself, five minutes. This is lesson 3's code with a synonym list added. Run it:

paras = {
    "A": "Full time employees receive 24 days of paid leave per year.",
    "B": "Leave requests must be approved by your manager.",
    "C": "The office cafeteria opens at 8 am.",
}
synonyms = {"holiday": "leave", "vacation": "leave"}

question = "How much holiday do I get?"
q = {synonyms.get(w, w) for w in question.lower().strip("?").split()}
for name, text in paras.items():
    words = set(text.lower().strip(".").split())
    print(name, len(q & words))

You should see A 1, B 1, C 0. The synonym list rescued "holiday", but now A and B are tied, and only A actually answers the question. Then change the question to "How much time off do I get?" and run it again. You get A 1, B 0, C 0. It looks like a win, but check why: the word "time" matched "full time employees", which has nothing to do with time off. Right paragraph, wrong reason. That is shape three from the lesson, and next time it will pick the wrong paragraph with the same confidence.

Then reply to the email. One line: "done", or the first word that confused you.
